quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results (CFO Jason Tsai, non-GAAP): sales 'increased 15% sequentially and over 45% year-on-year to $278.5 million', above the high end of guidance and 'surpassing our $1 billion target run rate set at the start of the year', on continued strength in mobile demand and strong growth in PCIe 5 client SSD. Gross margin rose to 49.2% on new products and a mix shift toward client PC; operating expenses rose to $83.2 million on investment in the AI/enterprise SSD and boot drive businesses; operating margin 19.3%; earnings per ADS $1.26. Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash were $277.1 million (vs $272.4 million at the end of Q3 2025) after $16.7 million of dividends and an inventory build to support the expected ramp.
quarterly_data.figure: $278.5 million (up 15% sequentially, over 45% year-on-year); gross margin 49.2%; operating margin 19.3%; earnings per ADS $1.26

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 outlook (CFO): revenue to 'grow 5% to 10% to $292 million to $306 million', up sequentially and 'counter to typical seasonality', with particular strength in mobile on market share gains. Gross margin guided slightly lower at 46% to 47% on product mix (mobile eMMC/UFS controllers run a little below corporate average), recovering to the 48% to 50% target range through the year as PCIe 5 controllers and enterprise SSD grow in the mix; operating margin 16% to 18%. CEO: Q1 revenue 'will be the lowest of 2026', with sequential growth through the rest of the year and 2026 expected to be the highest annual revenue in company history (no full-year revenue guidance given). CFO: tapeout and development costs, especially the 4-nanometer tapeout, lift opex in Q2 and Q3, but full-year 2026 operating margin is expected to improve versus 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 revenue $292 million to $306 million (5% to 10%); gross margin 46% to 47%; operating margin 16% to 18%

quarterly_data.signal: NAND/DRAM scarcity: CEO Wallace Kou said 'AI CSPs has attempt to lock up all the DRAM and NAND supply through 2026', making it hard for other buyers to get product and driving 'significant intra-quarter price increases'. NAND makers are shifting internal resources and capex to DRAM, HBM and customized AI memory, and new NAND capacity is limited by land, clean room and equipment lead times. The shortage is 'much more severe than anybody can imagine because CSP really demand much more than the current supply can support'; even leading smartphone makers struggle to procure NAND and LPDDR5, and many automotive Tier 1 suppliers (the lowest priority for NAND and DRAM makers) are asking Silicon Motion for help. Silicon Motion has no long-term supply agreement ('we did not have the LTA agreement') and relies on its NAND maker relationships; it takes NAND-bundled business case by case and may skip business whose margin misses the company target.
quarterly_data.figure: AI CSPs locking up DRAM and NAND supply through 2026; no LTA agreement

quarterly_data.signal: MonTitan enterprise SSD controllers: in the December quarter Silicon Motion began end-user qualification of TLC-based high-performance compute SSDs using MonTitan with multiple customers; qualification runs through the first half of 2026 with commercial ramp in the second half. High-capacity QLC storage SSDs, 'the largest addressable market for MonTitan', remain on track to begin qualification with multiple customers this year; QLC demand has accelerated given the current HDD supply shortage, and management expects QLC SSDs to become a compelling alternative to HDD. Management 'remain confident that MonTitan will ramp to represent at least 5% to 10% of revenue, exiting 2026' - a MonTitan-controller-only figure that excludes boot drive solutions (MonTitan is reported in the controller business). The CEO tied fast-growing AI inference (KV cache, latency, capacity) to storage demand that will 'all need MonTitan to fill the role'.
quarterly_data.figure: at least 5% to 10% of revenue, exiting 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Next-generation MonTitan: during 2026 Silicon Motion plans to tape out its first 4-nanometer chip, a PCIe 6 version of MonTitan targeting hyperscalers, NAND flash makers, storage system providers, CSPs and other Tier 1 customers, developed with multiple partner customers. Design wins are already secured with multiple Tier 1 customers; the controller should drive MonTitan success 'beginning in the 2027, '28 time frame' and is 'expected to ramp significantly in 2028'. CFO (point-in-time plan): the 'upcoming 4-nanometer tapeout in the second quarter' will drive higher operating expenses in the second and third quarters of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: 4-nanometer PCIe 6 tapeout in the second quarter; ramp significantly in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Enterprise boot drive storage (a complete SSD, so Silicon Motion must procure NAND) is 'rapidly evolving into a significant new era of growth'. CEO on the DPU boot-drive business: 'We see this year revenue relatively around $50 million but I think next year will be much higher', depending on NAND procurement and on passing incremental cost through with a meaningful margin; Silicon Motion is 'not the sole supplier for the DPU program' (leading CPU and GPU makers use 2 or 3 suppliers) and has multiple programs and customers beyond one GPU customer, with some new programs ramping from Q4. It is also working with a 'leading search engine company' on an enterprise-grade boot storage drive. Boot drives are reported in SSD solutions and are not in the MonTitan 5% to 10% target. NAND is bought at market price with pass-through negotiated quarter by quarter, which will weigh on gross margin; as a strategic business it may run below the corporate average margin. On supply: 'Currently, we have 2 NAND supplier. One is secure but the other is not.'
quarterly_data.figure: relatively around $50 million boot drive revenue this year; 2 NAND supplier (one secure)

quarterly_data.signal: Mobile eMMC/UFS: NAND makers are exiting mobile in favor of DRAM and HBM ('2 NAND makers walked away from the mobile storage') while still selling wafers to module makers, most of which use Silicon Motion controllers with US, Japanese and local Chinese NAND. eMMC/UFS 'grew 25% for the full year' 2025, far outperforming the smartphone embedded market, and Silicon Motion says it is 'the only meaningful merchant controller maker for the eMMC and UFS'; the eMMC market ships 'over 900 million units' annually as flash makers have all but exited it. For 2026 the CEO expects mobile controllers to 'exceed probably about 35%, 40% of our total company revenue', split roughly half smartphone and half non-smartphone, with a high-end ramp expected by end of 2026. Chinese controller rivals are constrained because advanced nodes (7, 6 and 5 nanometer) need approval from TSMC or Samsung, while local Chinese fabs handle only 22/28 nanometer legacy products.
quarterly_data.figure: eMMC, UFS grew 25% in 2025; mobile controllers to exceed probably about 35%, 40% of 2026 company revenue; eMMC market over 900 million units shipped annually

quarterly_data.signal: Client SSD: 2025 was a turning point on the 8-channel PCIe 5 controller (4 flash maker partners and nearly all module makers), setting a path to lift client PC share 'from 30% today to 40% over the next few years'. The new DRAM-less 4-channel PCIe 5 controller has design wins with 4 NAND flash makers, 'including the 2 from South Korea', and should ramp significantly through 2026, especially in the second half, because the DRAM shortage will slow 8-channel high-end PCIe 5 adoption 'dramatically in 2026'. The CEO expects 2026 PC unit shipments to decline 5% to 10% with value-line storage despec, but NAND makers moving allocation to CSPs lets module makers (mostly Silicon Motion design wins) fill the gap; CFO: even the 4-channel PCIe 5 part carries 'a much higher ASP than a comparable PCIe 4', so share and ASP both rise in 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: client PC share from 30% today to 40%; 2026 PC unit shipment decline 5% to 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Ferri automotive/industrial storage: strong demand as customers rely on Silicon Motion for steady supply in the tight NAND market; management expects 'the ramp of automotive business to about 10% of total business by the end of this year', balancing revenue growth with margin stability and taking NAND-bundled automotive business only where incremental cost can be passed through to the automotive supply chain.
quarterly_data.figure: automotive about 10% of total business by the end of this year

connects_to.relationship: DRAM-less enterprise Boot Drive storage for BlueField DPUs

contracts.signal: Boot drives for 'the leading AI GPU maker' (management did not name the customer; an analyst asked about BlueField and the CEO answered on it): volume shipments for 'their current DPU product' started in the fourth quarter of 2025, and Silicon Motion is qualifying the next-generation DPU plus 'several NVLink and Ethernet switches of their new GPU/CPU platform' expected to launch in the second half of 2026, which need higher capacities with much higher ASP and unit volume. CEO: 'BlueField-3 is for -- primarily for this year' and the NVLink and Ethernet switches are 'for the second half and really more volume in 2027'. CFO expects next-generation DPU revenue 'sometime in the back half of the year'. The customer uses 2 to 3 suppliers, so Silicon Motion is not the sole DPU boot-drive supplier.
contracts.type: supply (boot drive volume shipments + next-generation qualification)
